tasks.question: Why does geopandas legend rendering fail to scale efficiently when plotting categorical data with large numbers of unique categories in both static and interactive visualization modes?
tasks.reference_answer: GeoPandas legend rendering scales poorly for high cardinality categorical columns because both its Matplotlib and Folium based code paths implement categorical legends by explicitly generating one legend entry per category, which makes the computational cost, memory usage, and rendering overhead grow linearly with the number of unique values rather than with the visual complexity of the geometries themselves; in the static plotting path, once a column is detected as categorical, GeoPandas converts it to a pandas Categorical, extracts all category labels, and defines the color index span to cover the full category range, for example `categories = list(cat.categories)` followed by `vmax = len(categories) - 1` (geopandas/plotting.py L795–L807), and when `legend=True` it constructs the legend by iterating over the entire category list, creating a separate Matplotlib artist for each category via logic equivalent to `for i in range(len(categories)):` with one handle per label, before passing the full handle and label lists into `ax.legend` and triggering a redraw with `ax.figure.canvas.draw_idle()` (geopandas/plotting.py L910–L946, L956), so thousands of categories directly translate into thousands of Python objects and an expensive layout computation inside Matplotlib; in the interactive `explore` path, the same fundamental design choice appears, where the data are coerced to a Categorical and the number of legend entries is fixed as `N = len(cat.categories)` (geopandas/explore.py L442–L445), colors are computed for every category index using the colormap, and the categorical legend HTML is built by concatenating one HTML fragment per category in a loop equivalent to `for label, color in zip(categories, colors): body += ...`, which is then injected into the Leaflet map (geopandas/explore.py L446–L460, L890–L902); because neither implementation introduces any aggregation, truncation, or deferred rendering of legend entries, legend construction becomes O(n) in both Python level work and rendering complexity, and with large numbers of categories the legend itself dominates performance and display cost even though the underlying spatial plotting logic remains unchanged.

tasks.question: Why does the interactive explore() method experience performance degradation and high CPU consumption when rendering large GeoDataFrames with complex styling and multiple layers?

After serialization, explore() sets up styling and interactivity by constructing style functions, tooltips, popups, and highlight logic that are evaluated per feature, which is implemented in geopandas/explore.py around lines 511 to 669, so choropleths and complex styling multiply computation by the number of geometries. When multiple layers are added, this same serialization and styling pipeline runs independently for each layer, further compounding the cost. Finally, on the client side, Leaflet must parse the full GeoJSON, create and draw a vector object for each feature, and attach interaction handlers, so large numbers of features or highly detailed geometries significantly increase browser side CPU load. Together, the eager GeoJSON serialization, per feature styling logic, repeated layer processing, and Leaflet’s vector rendering model explain why explore() degrades in performance and becomes CPU intensive for large, richly styled GeoDataFrames.
